title: How can a jacket be waterproof and breathable?
teaches: Rubberised cloth from Macintosh (1823) and vulcanised rubber; gabardine and waxed cotton; water-repellent finishes and PFAS; coated nylon; Gore-Tex's microporous membrane (1976) and its limits; Stephanie Kwolek and Kevlar

blocks.text: A plastic poncho keeps rain out completely, but after an hour of walking uphill in one, the wearer is soaked with sweat. A good hiking jacket keeps out the rain and lets most of that sweat escape. In this lesson we look at how waterproof cloth developed, from rubber to modern membranes, what "breathable" means, which is letting sweat escape as vapour, and how far it can go.

In 1823 the Scottish chemist **Charles Macintosh** patented a waterproof cloth. He dissolved natural rubber in naphtha, a by-product of making coal gas, spread it between two layers of cotton and pressed them together. Coats of the cloth became known as mackintoshes. Early rubber had two faults: it turned sticky in summer and stiff in winter, and it smelt. In the 1840s Charles Goodyear in the United States and Thomas Hancock in England found that heating rubber with sulphur, **vulcanisation**, made it stable over a wide range of temperatures, and rubberised cloth became practical.

A rubber coat keeps out rain completely, and it keeps in sweat just as completely. Other makers chose a compromise. In 1879 Thomas Burberry, a draper in Hampshire, developed **gabardine**, a tightly woven twill of cotton yarn treated to repel water before weaving. Rain ran off it, while air and vapour could still pass between the fibres. Sailors, farmers and motorcyclists wore **waxed cotton**, a dense cotton cloth soaked in oil or wax, which kept out rain until the wax wore thin and was rubbed in again. The wax filled most of the gaps, so it let out less vapour than gabardine. A **windproof shell** with no barrier at all lets vapour out freely but lets rain through.

Most modern outdoor clothing has an outer cloth treated with a **durable water repellent**, a finish that makes water bead up and roll off instead of soaking in. Water spreads into cotton or nylon because it is attracted to the fibre surface; a repellent finish lowers that attraction so the drop stays round. For decades the most effective finishes were fluorinated chemicals, related to the coating on non-stick pans. Some of these compounds, known together as **PFAS** (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances), do not break down in the environment and have been found in water, wildlife and human blood around the world. The European Union, several US states and major outdoor brands have restricted or abandoned them, and most finishes now use other chemistry that is less durable.

Repellent cloth on its own is not waterproof. Under pressure, such as the weight of a rucksack strap pressing a wet shoulder or a knee on wet ground, water is pushed through the gaps between threads. A fully waterproof jacket needs a continuous barrier behind the outer cloth, and the cheapest barrier is a coating of polyurethane on nylon. A solid coating lets very little vapour through, so a coated nylon jacket behaves much like a rubber one in hard work.

In 1969 **Bob Gore**, working in his family's company in Delaware, found that PTFE, the plastic of non-stick coatings, polytetrafluoroethylene, could be stretched suddenly into a thin film full of tiny pores. In this **microporous** film each pore is far too small for a drop of liquid water to pass. PTFE repels water so strongly that it would take a great deal of pressure to force water into such a narrow opening. A single water molecule in sweat vapour, though, is hundreds of times narrower than the pores and passes through freely. Gore and his company launched the membrane in outdoor clothing in 1976 as **Gore-Tex**, laminated between an outer nylon and an inner lining.

A membrane lets vapour out only as fast as it diffuses from the warm, humid air inside the jacket to the cooler, drier air outside. Laboratory tests give jackets impressive ratings, but on a hillside in steady rain the outer cloth is wet and cold, the air is already humid, and the flow is much slower. A body working hard can make more sweat than a membrane lets out, and the extra vapour condenses into water inside the jacket.

blocks.task: Find when the membrane keeps you dry, and when it cannot

blocks.text: Jacket makers add underarm zips, called pit zips, and mesh-lined pockets so that the wearer can let warm, humid air out directly when working hard. Since 2022 Gore has also sold membranes made of expanded polyethylene in place of PTFE, to avoid the fluorinated chemicals used in making PTFE.

Another fibre from the same era protects in a different way. In 1965 **Stephanie Kwolek**, a chemist at DuPont searching for a light, strong fibre for car tyres, produced a polymer solution that was thin and cloudy instead of thick and clear, as polymer solutions usually were. Colleagues were reluctant to spin it, expecting it to clog the spinneret, but she persuaded a technician to try. The long, stiff chains of the polymer lay aligned in bundles in the solution, like logs on a river, and these ordered patches scattered light, which made it cloudy. The fibre spun from it was five times as strong as steel for its weight.

DuPont sold the fibre from 1971 as **Kevlar**. It went into tyres, ropes and boat hulls, and into bulletproof vests, in which many layers of tightly woven Kevlar spread the force of a bullet across the whole vest and stop it. Kwolek was among the first women elected to the US National Inventors Hall of Fame, in 1995.

items.ask: What did vulcanisation fix in rubberised cloth?
choices: Rubber turning sticky in heat and stiff in cold
Rubber letting rain through in heavy storms
Rubber being too expensive for coats
Rubber trapping sweat inside the coat
items.why: Heating rubber with sulphur made it stable across a wide range of temperatures. It still trapped sweat.

items.ask: How does a microporous membrane keep rain out but let sweat out?
choices: Its pores block liquid drops but pass single vapour molecules
It absorbs rain and releases it as vapour
It heats the rain until it evaporates
Its pores open in dry air and close in rain
items.why: Water-repellent pores are far too small for liquid water to be forced in, but vapour molecules pass easily.

items.ask: Why can a hiker get wet inside a membrane jacket?
choices: Hard work makes sweat faster than vapour can escape
The membrane lets rain in under heavy use
The membrane absorbs sweat and swells shut
Membranes only work in warm, dry weather
items.why: Vapour escapes only as fast as it diffuses out. Excess sweat condenses inside the jacket.

items.ask: What was unusual about the solution Kwolek spun into Kevlar?
choices: It was thin and cloudy, with aligned stiff chains
It was made entirely from natural plant fibre
It had to be spun at very low temperature
It was a solid that was cut into threads
items.why: The stiff chains lined up in the solution, which made it cloudy and gave a very strong fibre.

summary: **Macintosh rubberised cloth in 1823.** Rubber between two cottons kept rain out and sweat in.
**Vulcanisation made rubber stable.** Sulphur and heat stopped it turning sticky or stiff.
**Gabardine and waxed cotton compromised.** A tight, treated weave or a coat of wax shed rain; gabardine also let vapour out.
**Repellent finishes bead water.** The best were fluorinated PFAS, now being phased out.
**A membrane has pores of a useful size.** Too small for liquid drops, far bigger than vapour molecules.
**Breathability has limits.** Hard work makes more sweat than a membrane can let out.
**Kwolek made Kevlar.** Aligned stiff chains gave a fibre five times as strong as steel for its weight.
